newsitem.title: UK: BOE correct to cool British rate demands-economists.
newsitem.headline: BOE correct to cool British rate demands-economists.

text.p: The Bank of England has toned down its demands for higher interest rates and is right to do so, economists said on Tuesday.
The Bank has finally accepted that a powerful rally from the pound has subdued inflation in the short-term, something it had been reluctant to recognise until now.

Its change of heart will allow Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke to leave base rates on hold at six percent until the election, due by May, safe in the knowledge that markets see it as economically justified, not just politically expedient.

"The Bank of England has been barking up the wrong tree," said Nigel Richardson, head of bond research at Yamaichi International. "Over the short-term, sterling can and does have an effect on inflation."

The pound -- which has rocketed by around 16 percent since last August -- has a dual effect on the economy, cutting import prices and putting a brake on inflation, and also hurting British exporters by pushing their prices higher.
But it was not until last week that the Bank accepted in its inflation report the threat of inflation had receded, in the short-term at least.

On Monday, Bank governor Eddie George told parliament's Treasury Select Committee that a spate of weaker UK economic data, along with the pound's strength, had made the need for an interest rise less urgent than was thought in December.

He denied that this represented a softening of the Bank's stance but said it was possible the soaring pound could push underlying inflation down to the government's 2.5 percent target in the months ahead.
It stood at 3.1 percent year-on-year in January.

That is a very different tune to the one George sang at his December monetary meeting with Clarke. Then, he said if interest rates did not rise immediately by a quarter-point, the economy would require a half-point increase early in 1997.

"Two things have happened since then. The exchange rate has gone further and the acceleration in the data that was apparent in October and November has not persisted. That makes it (a rate rise) absolutely less pressing than it was," George said.
Base rates have been held at six percent since October.

Clarke will breathe a sigh of relief that he can avoid a full blown row with his key monetary adviser before the election. And allegations that he has left rates on hold in an attempt to boost the Conservative government's flagging fortunes will also lose their bite.
James McKay, economist at PaineWebber, said the Bank may still have further to go to get its view on the exchange rate right. To date, it has only recognised the short-term effect on price pressures.
"Exporters are coming under pressure and job security and income will be affected into the medium-term. The economy is likely to turn out a lot slower than most people anticipate."
Richardson said he was in the middle of the two camps -- one demanding rate rises now and the other saying inflation is dead and buried.
"The Bank is right that there is a high level of demand in the economy which could fuel inflation further out," he said. And there is always the risk that the pound's rally reverses.
"But until now, the Bank had lost the plot over the short-term. Rates will have to go up, but there is no hurry."
The financial markets, in the shape of interest rate futures, have certainly scaled back their rate expectations.

At the turn of the year, June short sterling was close to pricing in base rates at seven percent by the end of June. Now at 93.58, the contract is positioned for no more than a 25 basis point rate rise before the second half of the year.
That looks about right, McKay said. "George has clearly softened his stance in terms of rates. He's now looking for only a quarter-point hike and is not too pushy about the timing."
